stories.title: A Receipt for a Chair
stories.text:
This is {dj}, keeping you company on {station}. Got a little story tonight about a receipt. Not a map to buried caps. Not a password. Just a receipt for one wooden chair.

A woman named Ada came through Goodneighbor with it folded inside a tobacco tin. The paper had gone the color of old teeth. Most of the ink was gone, too, but you could still make out a price, a date, and two words somebody had written across the bottom: paid, delivered.

She said her father had made the chair. Sold it before the war, if the date was right. Ada was a ghoul, and the date might have been right, but she admitted her memory had started putting different summers in the same drawer. Sometimes she remembered the customer wearing a blue coat. Sometimes brown. Always remembered him asking if the chair would hold a large man.

Her father had said it would hold a small family if they sat politely.

Now, Ada wasn't looking for a fortune. She wanted the chair. Said there'd been a little crooked star carved underneath the seat. Her father put one on everything he made. His hands shook by the end, but that star always came out clean.

People told her to forget it. Two hundred years is a long delivery route. Wood burns. Roofs fall. Folks get cold and quit asking what used to belong to whom.

But she kept that receipt. Kept asking.

One wet evening, a trader brought in a chair tied across the back of his pack. Three legs were original. The fourth looked like it had spent a previous life as a broom. He wanted twelve caps for it, then fifteen after somebody sat down and discovered it didn't collapse.

Ada asked to turn it over.

The star was there.

The trader saw her face and stopped talking about the price. That was a kind thing. He could have doubled it. Plenty would have. Instead, he asked why she wanted a chair with somebody else's repairs on it.

She ran her hand along the seat. There were knife marks. A little round burn. One deep scratch where something heavy had been dragged across it.

Then she laughed. Soft at first, like a match that hadn't decided whether to catch.

She said, 'Because they used it.'

That was all. They used it. Somebody had sat in her father's chair long enough to wear a shallow place into the wood. Somebody had broken a leg and bothered to make another. The world had ended, and somewhere in all that ending, somebody still thought the chair was worth fixing.

She paid him fifteen caps. Didn't even show the receipt.

A few nights later, I saw it outside her door. A neighbor was sitting in it, working a stone out of his boot. Ada was standing beside him with two cups of something hot. That chair wasn't a shrine. Wasn't waiting for the right person to deserve it. It was holding a tired man while he got ready to walk again.

You can spend a whole life wondering if anything you made will matter after you're gone. Maybe the answer doesn't come with your name on it. Maybe it comes with a broom handle for a leg and somebody who finally gets to sit down.

That's my story tonight. If you've got something worth mending, don't wait for the world to become a better place first. Pull it close. Find your tools. We'll keep a little music on while you work.

stories.title: The Radio That Listened
stories.text:
You're listening to {station}. {dj} here. There's a particular sound an empty room makes when a radio stops working. You don't notice it until the music's gone. Then every pipe, every loose window, every footstep outside starts taking its turn.

There was a repairman folks called Finch who understood that sound better than most. Worked out of a room so narrow he had to open the door before he could change his mind. Had a bench, a lamp, and a coffee tin full of screws that never seemed to fit anything currently broken.

One afternoon a woman brought him a little radio wrapped in a dish towel. Said it had belonged to her brother. Said she'd dropped it, which was true, but didn't say she'd dropped it while packing his things after he died. Finch didn't ask why the towel was clean and everything else she carried was covered in road dust.

He told her to come back in three days.

Well, three days went by. Then four. She came in angry on the fifth, and there was her radio on the bench, open like a little metal patient. Finch had found the broken connection. Easy enough. He'd also found a paper note folded behind the speaker.

It said: If you get home first, leave it on.

No name. No date. Just that.

He hadn't known whether to put it back. Hadn't wanted to make the decision for her. So he'd done what a lot of decent people do when they don't know the right thing. He'd made himself busy with the wrong thing. Cleaned every contact. Straightened the bent aerial. Fixed a knob that hadn't needed fixing.

She read the note twice. Then she sat down on a crate and told him about her brother.

Not the grand stories. Not the brave things you tell a room full of people. She told Finch how her brother ate the burnt piece of anything because he said it had more character. How he whistled when he was trying to remember where he'd put a tool. How he could sleep through a firefight but woke up furious if somebody moved his cup.

Finch listened. Didn't offer to explain what any of it meant. Didn't tell her time would fix it. Just listened until the light in his window went from gray to yellow.

Then he connected the last wire.

The speaker gave a little crackle. A voice came through, complaining about the weather somewhere neither of them had been. She laughed at the foolishness of it. All that waiting, all that sorrow, and the first thing the radio had to say was that it might rain.

She asked what she owed him.

He charged her for the wire. Two caps. Said the rest had been work he chose to do.

Now, that doesn't make Finch a saint. He still overcharged a fellow who tried to pay him with a jar of dubious mushrooms. Still complained when people leaned on his door. But after that, there was always a spare crate beside his bench. Nobody could remember him putting it there. Everybody knew what it was for.

Sometimes people don't bring you the thing that's broken. They bring you the thing they can bear to put on a table.

If somebody does that tonight, leave a little room beside you. You don't have to know how to fix everything. A chair, a cup, a few minutes without looking at the door. There's a kind of repair in that, too.

Stay with me. We've got another record coming, and for a little while this old radio can do the talking.

stories.title: The Bear at Mile Marker Nine
stories.text:
This is {dj}, and you're listening to {station}. Before the next record, I need to tell you about a teddy bear. You may laugh now. I'd prefer you got it out of your system before we reach the part involving the teeth.

A caravan guard I know found the bear sitting on a roadside marker. No caravan wreck. No little campsite. Just a brown bear with a blue ribbon, looking straight down the road like it expected somebody to be late.

He passed it at dawn. Passed it again that afternoon on his way back. Same marker. Different ribbon. Red this time.

Now, a sensible man would say somebody changed the ribbon. A less sensible man would ask why. My friend was sensible enough to keep walking and curious enough to come tell me. Dangerous combination. Most of our trouble begins with that particular mixture.

We went back the next morning. The bear was gone. In its place was a tooth.

Not a claw. Not something you could blame on a dog. A little human molar, clean as a dinner plate. My friend wanted to leave immediately. I respected his position, which is why I asked him to wait a hundred feet away instead of calling him a coward.

There were scratches on the back of the marker. Three groups of little lines. Below them, somebody had pushed a strip of cloth into a crack. Blue on one end. Red on the other.

I spent two nights staring at that strip. Made a beautiful chart. Connected routes, departure times, missing traders, prices of ammunition. I had arrows pointing at things that had never previously been accused of pointing anywhere. By sunrise, my chart explained everything except the tooth.

Then an old scavenger looked at it and said, 'That's a child's ribbon.'

I told her I'd established that.

She said, 'No. I mean it's been cut into measuring lengths. Look at the knots.'

She was right. Blue meant the road was clear. Red meant wait. The scratches counted wagons. Somebody was using a toy to signal people who knew where to look.

That still leaves the tooth, neighbor. I haven't forgotten the tooth.

We watched the marker from a busted drainage pipe the following evening. A boy came out of the brush carrying the bear. Maybe fourteen. Hard to judge an age when hunger's been doing the growing. He changed the ribbon, checked the road, and tucked something under the bear's paw.

My friend stepped out before I could stop him. Asked the boy about the tooth.

The boy said, 'Payment.'

Then he ran.

We found a tiny tin under the paw. Two more teeth inside. And a scrap of paper with one word written on it: enough.

I won't tell you what that means. I don't know. Could be children keeping a count. Could be a cruel little joke. Could be somebody paying a price we haven't learned how to name yet. I haven't seen an Institute agent, a secret transmitter, or a machine in the bear. If I tell you otherwise, I become another fellow selling certainty he hasn't earned.

But the marker's empty now. The caravan guard changed his route. And yesterday, somebody left a blue ribbon looped around the handle of my door.

So here's what I know. A toy can be a signal. A road can have rules nobody told you. And when a child says 'payment,' you ought to find out who's collecting before you decide you've heard a funny story.

Keep your eyes open. Keep your conclusions separate from your evidence. And if you see that bear, don't move it just to prove you're brave. There's another record coming. I need a minute to think.

stories.title: A Red Coat in an Empty Window
stories.text:
You're on {station}. {dj} here. Tonight's report concerns a red coat, an empty shop, and a perfectly reasonable explanation that kept getting less reasonable every time somebody repeated it.

The shop had a mannequin in the window. Nothing remarkable about that. Half the Commonwealth still has plastic people standing where real people used to argue about prices. This one wore a red coat, one glove, and a hat with a brim somebody had carefully repaired.

A courier noticed it because she passed that window every other day. On Monday, the mannequin faced the road. On Wednesday, it faced the door. Friday, it was looking into the back of the shop.

She told me people had started calling it haunted.

I said haunting was a lazy explanation. You don't need a ghost when you've got hinges, fishing line, and a neighbor with too much free time. We went inside and found none of those things. Also found no footprints, which would have impressed me more if the floor hadn't been entirely covered in wet leaves.

There was, however, a dry circle beneath the mannequin's stand.

Somebody had lifted it recently.

The courier said that settled it. Somebody moving a mannequin. I agreed. Then I asked what, precisely, it settled. She gave me the look people give a radio host when they remember they could have kept walking.

We returned after dark. Waited across the street. A man came to the shop carrying a lantern and a loaf of bread. Sat down beside the mannequin. Talked for twenty minutes. Couldn't hear the words. When he left, he turned it toward the door.

The next morning, I asked him about it.

He said the coat had belonged to his wife.

I put my notebook away. There are moments when a person ought to know how to do that.

He told me she'd always wanted a shop with a window. Said she'd turn a chair to face the door whenever he went out, so she'd see him coming home. After she died, he'd found the coat, found the mannequin, and made something he could talk to without having to explain himself to another living soul.

That should have been the end. A sad story, a quiet kindness, and your host learning to mind his business. I'd even begun composing an unusually modest apology.

Then the courier came back.

She'd seen somebody else at the window. A woman wearing a gray scarf, taking the red coat off the mannequin and putting it on. The courier followed her as far as a ruined overpass. Lost her there. Found the coat back in the window the following morning.

I asked the man if anybody borrowed it. He said no. I asked whether his wife had worn a gray scarf. He said everybody wore scarves when the cold got bad. Didn't look at the window when he said it.

Here are the facts. A grieving man visits an empty shop. Somebody else may be using it. A courier saw a woman, and a red coat came back. That isn't proof of a ghost. Isn't proof of a synth, either. It's proof that two people can look at the same window and bring home entirely different questions.

We're watching the road. We are leaving the coat alone. If the woman comes back, we're going to ask her name before deciding what kind of thing she is.

That's a radical investigative technique, I realize. Might catch on if it doesn't get us killed. Stay tuned. The next song has fewer witnesses to interview.
